bivy.name: Dailey Prairie road end (staging and bike stash, not a camp)
bivy.notes: This old prairie is where the logging road system tops out and the climbers path to the west ridge of North Twin begins, roughly five miles and two thousand feet of road above the river bridge. Almost every party bikes to here and leaves the bike, which turns a brutal road walk into a fast coast on the way out. It reads like the obvious basecamp and it is not one: under the current landowner rules this ground is day use only, no camping and no fire, and vehicles must never block the road or the gate. Treat it as a staging point where you shoulder the pack for the last three thousand feet, and push on to the wilderness ground above if you want to sleep out. Snow lingers on the path above roughly four thousand feet well into early summer. The road is also subject to closure on short notice for active logging, quarry work or fire danger, and signs posting a closure have appeared with no warning.
bivy.water: None reliable at the prairie itself; carry what you need up from the valley
bivy.permit: Private industrial timberland. The gate at the Middle Fork river bridge is locked and keys are no longer issued for this northern entrance, so the road is foot and bicycle only. The landowner now runs a fee recreation permit covering this block of forestland, with a hard cap on the number of non-motorized permits issued, daylight-only entry of roughly an hour and a half either side of sunrise and sunset, no campfires at any time, and no camping. Ownership of these roads has changed hands more than once and the terms have changed with it, so confirm the current permit and gate situation with the landowner before you go rather than assuming older terms still apply.
bivy.capacity: Open ground with room for several parties, but overnight use is not permitted

bivy.name: Orsino Creek Basin
bivy.notes: This is the standard overnight camp for the west ridge of South Twin and the most useful water stop on the whole northwest approach. It is reached from the Dailey Prairie road system by crossing Orsino Creek and following a brushy old road that fades into a path through timber, then traversing up red talus past the ruins of an old cabin into the basin. From the camp a steep and thoroughly unpleasant slog up dirt, scree and talus gains an obvious notch on the west ridge at around five thousand two hundred feet. The ground is coarse and drains fast, so pitch on the flat gravel benches rather than hunting for soft ground. Fill everything here. Above this point the only water is snowmelt and glacier runoff, and in a dry August there may be none at all. Best from July through September; earlier the basin holds snow and the creek runs high and cold.
bivy.water: Orsino Creek, the most reliable water on the west side of the range. It is the last dependable source for the summits and for the higher camps, and it shrinks noticeably by late summer
bivy.permit: The basin sits close to the boundary between private timberland below and national forest wilderness above. Camping is legal on the forest side and not on the timber company side, and the line is not signed on the ground, so camp high in the basin rather than low. No overnight permit is currently required on the forest side; standard wilderness rules apply, including a party size limit of twelve. Campfires are a poor idea anywhere here and are banned outright on the private ground below; late summer fire restrictions are routine.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small dispersed sites among talus and heather; two to three tents

Best from July through September; earlier the basin holds snow and the creek runs high and cold.

bivy.water: Side streams and snowmelt near camp, but they are seasonal and can dry or go silty by late summer — treat everything and carry a reserve on a hot September approach
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mount Baker Wilderness) — NO North Cascades National Park permit needed here, since the park boundary is still ahead at the pass. What you need is a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Hannegan trailhead; a Washington Discover Pass is NOT valid at this Forest Service fee site.
bivy.capacity: A handful of designated tent spots with a shared cooking area and a backcountry toilet; a second toilet sits at the pass itself

bivy.name: Boundary Camp
bivy.notes: Boundary sits just over Hannegan Pass at the line where Forest Service ground becomes national park, which is exactly why it trips people up: you park under a Northwest Forest Pass and then sleep under an NPS permit. With only three sites it books out on summer weekends, and a party arriving without a reservation has no legal fallback nearby. It is the natural first night for anything heading down the Chilliwack or up onto Copper Ridge. Fire closures in 2026 affected camps and trails on this side of the pass, so check the park's current closure page rather than assuming a reservation implies open ground.
bivy.water: A nearby subalpine stream normally runs through the climbing season, though it is a snowmelt source and thins out late
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, obtained through the park's reservation system and picked up in person at Marblemount. Campfires are not allowed here.
bivy.capacity: Three designated sites, each rated for up to four people, with a pit toilet

bivy.name: Copper Lake Camp, Copper Ridge
bivy.notes: Of the three camps strung along Copper Ridge, this is the one that solves water: the others are drier, and one is normally described as having no water source at all, which forces a long carry from lower down. That makes it the sensible high camp for anyone using the ridge as a high traverse toward the Chilliwack drainage rather than dropping straight into the valley. The ridge is exposed and the sites are small, so a party of more than four has to split across permits. Copper Ridge and the wider Copper Loop were inside the 2026 fire closure footprint, and burned ground stays hazardous for years afterward.
bivy.water: The lake is immediately at hand and reliable all season — a real advantage on this ridge
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, picked up at Marblemount. Food, rubbish and scented items must go in the provided lockers or an approved canister.
bivy.capacity: Designated sites for parties of up to four, with a composting toilet and food-storage lockers

bivy.name: US Cabin Camp, Chilliwack River
bivy.notes: A deep-forest valley camp rather than a climbing bivy, and its value is positional — it is roughly where a party bound for Bear Mountain or the peaks further up the drainage stops before leaving the trail. The lack of a food locker is worth planning around, because the neighbouring camps have them and it is easy to assume continuity. Old-growth valley bottom means it stays cool and damp, so expect wet gear in the morning. The Chilliwack River Trail was among the 2026 closures and its status should be confirmed before a trip is built around it.
bivy.water: The Chilliwack River is a few steps away and runs year round, though it carries glacial silt and needs filtering rather than just treating
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit from Marblemount. Unlike the ridge camps this one has NO food-storage hardware, so bring a canister or be prepared to hang.
bivy.capacity: Four sites, split between a pair near the trail and a pair down by the river, with a pit toilet

bivy.name: Basin below the Bear Mountain saddle
bivy.notes: The launching point for the north side of Bear Mountain, reached by leaving the Chilliwack valley trail and following a lightly marked line up the ridge toward treeline and then over into the basin. It is a long way in — most parties treat it as a second or third night rather than something reachable from the road — and the ground above the trail is faint enough that route-finding matters. accounts disagree on how usable the alternative approach from Chilliwack Lake in British Columbia is, with the cross-border stretch reported at times as heavy bushwhacking, so the length of the trail-based approach from Hannegan Pass is the price of certainty.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and tarns in the basin, reliable in early summer and can fail entirely by late season — carry water up if the year has been dry
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for a CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE rather than a designated camp, arranged at Marblemount. Zones are quota-limited with their own siting rules, so ask for the zone by name rather than assuming a valley camp reservation covers you.
bivy.capacity: Informal boulder-and-heather sites for a small party; no facilities of any kind

bivy.name: Boston Basin high camp
bivy.notes: The comfortable planned camp, roughly 6,300 to 6,400 ft on a sandy flat below a permanent snowfield, about three to four hours from the road. Everything on this route beyond it is committing, because the way onto the Boston Glacier goes over Sharkfin Col and that involves a rappel or a steep downclimb on poor rock that many parties describe as harder than the face itself. Coming back to this camp means reversing it. A lower camp at about 5,300 ft with its own composting toilet is the alternative if the upper sites are full.
bivy.water: Meltwater creeks and the permanent snowfield behind camp, reliable through the season
bivy.permit: A National Park Service backcountry permit is required. Boston Basin is one of the small number of zones that accepts advance reservations, and composting toilets serve both the upper and lower camp areas.
bivy.capacity: Hardened sites; the zone allows six parties per night and up to twelve people per party

bivy.name: Boston Glacier bivy
bivy.notes: A planned but fully exposed glacier bivy used to shorten summit day, on one of the largest glaciers in the lower 48. You are camping on a crevassed surface, so probe the platform and its surroundings before dropping the rope, and mark the perimeter. There is no shelter, no running water and no ground: everything is melted, and wind or a change in weather has nowhere to be dodged. The serious point is that it sits past Sharkfin Col — retreat from here means reclimbing that col, so committing to this bivy commits you to the route in a way that camping in Boston Basin does not.
bivy.water: Melted snow only
bivy.permit: The glacier is its own cross-country zone on the park permit system, capped at six people per party and six parties per night; human waste on snow and glacier terrain has to be packed out in a blue bag
bivy.capacity: Whatever platform you cut; the Boston Glacier cross-country zone allows six parties per night, six people per party

bivy.name: Sahale–Boston col bivy
bivy.notes: A tiny, spectacular perch on the col between Sahale and Boston, used by parties linking this face with other climbs in the basin or descending over Sahale Arm. It is an emergency-sized site, not a camp: there is room for one small tent, and cornices overhang the Davenport side, so probe out from the sleeping platform before settling in and do not wander in the dark. Wind exposure is total.
bivy.water: Melted snow
bivy.capacity: One small two-person tent's worth of flat ground

bivy.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
bivy.notes: Around 7,600 ft at the end of the Sahale Arm trail, about six miles and 4,000 ft from Cascade Pass trailhead. It is the standard base for the southwest side of Buckner: from camp you drop east onto Sahale's southeast ridge, scramble down easy ground to a snow finger, and cross into Horseshoe Basin before starting up. Marine fog rolling through the camp overnight is common and can leave you with no view of the objective until morning.
bivy.water: Streams of glacier runoff beside the camp; filter it. Late in a dry season the flow can be some distance down the moraine
bivy.permit: A North Cascades backcountry permit is required and is picked up in person at the Marblemount ranger station; the site is in heavy demand and reservations go through the park's lottery and booking system
bivy.capacity: A small number of built tent pads, each inside a low dry-stone wall — the walls exist because nothing shelters this ridge from wind. It is one of the most sought-after sites in the park

bivy.name: Upper Horseshoe Basin bivy
bivy.notes: A cross-country alternative used by parties who would rather not depend on a Sahale Glacier Camp permit: descend into the upper basin and sleep on whatever ground you reach. The basin is a mix of clean granite slabs, snow patches and loose rock, and the lower basin is the awkward part to travel. It puts you at the foot of the southwest slopes, but it is genuinely primitive and the slabs that look flat rarely are.
bivy.water: Snowmelt in the basin; a matter of what is running when you arrive rather than a fixed source
bivy.capacity: Informal — a party or two levelling a spot on slabs or snow, with no facilities of any kind

bivy.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside bivy
bivy.notes: The usual answer for a car-to-car day on this group, and the start of every west-side approach, roughly half a mile west of Washington Pass. Parties routinely sleep at the lot or at the highway hairpin rather than walking in, because the approaches are short enough that a high camp buys little. There are no facilities and no water; it is a place to sleep in or beside the car, not a campsite. Highway 20 is closed through the winter, so this is unavailable until the road reopens.
bivy.water: None at the trailhead. Carry what you need.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park
bivy.capacity: Informal, at the parking area — no prepared sites

bivy.name: Liberty Bell basin dispersed sites
bivy.notes: Sites in the basin on the west side of the group, reached by following the Blue Lake trail and then the signed climbers' path that branches off it toward the group. Worth it if you want to be under the west-side routes at first light rather than walking up from the road. Note the separate restriction around Blue Lake itself, where overnight camping is not allowed within a quarter mile of the lake — the basin sites are the ones to aim for, not the lakeshore. Treat it as a basin camp below the spires rather than a fixed spot.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and seasonal runoff in the basin — unreliable once the snow has gone
bivy.permit: No permit for dispersed camping; this is national forest, not the national park

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground
bivy.notes: The closest developed campground, about a ten-minute drive east down the highway from the Blue Lake trailhead, in the trees along Early Winters Creek. No reservations, so it is a gamble on a summer weekend. Its season runs roughly from late spring into autumn and is decided by snow rather than by a date.
bivy.water: Early Winters Creek runs through the campground
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fee

bivy.name: Klipchuck Campground
bivy.notes: Further east and lower than Lone Fir, which means it opens earlier in the season when the higher options are still under snow — the practical choice for an early-season trip. It sits far enough off the highway to be quiet and has more plumbing than anything nearer the climbing. The trade is a longer drive to the trailhead each morning. Check current status before relying on it; the highway-corridor campgrounds take periodic maintenance closures.
bivy.water: Piped water, sinks and flush toilets
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fee

bivy.name: Cutthroat Creek trailhead
bivy.notes: The lot sits a mile up the forest road from SR 20 and has a vault toilet but no water. Parties climbing the South Buttress or Southeast Buttress routinely sleep here or in a pullout on the road in before a pre-dawn start, though the lot itself is signed for day use and how strictly that is read varies; dispersed camping in the trees along the forest road below is the uncontroversial option. Access is entirely gated by the SR 20 winter closure, and the road has been shut for construction windows in recent seasons, so confirm before driving out.
bivy.water: None — no potable water at the trailhead. Cutthroat Creek runs below the lot and needs filtering.
bivy.permit: No camping permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day pass covers parking. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, NOT the national park, so there is no backcountry permit system here at all.
bivy.capacity: Large gravel lot, roughly 20-30 vehicles; fills on summer weekends with larch-season hikers

bivy.name: Cutthroat Lake basin, outside the quarter-mile closure
bivy.notes: The lake sits about 1.8 miles in with roughly 500 ft of gain, in the basin under the peak's north and east sides. It is a pleasant place to stage, but the quarter-mile closure exists because the shoreline was being loved to death and it is enforced rather than advisory. For a climb of the south side you gain nothing by coming here — the climbers' path branches off well before the lake — so treat it as a rest-day or bad-weather option rather than a staging camp.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet stream are dependable all season. Treat or filter.
bivy.permit: No permit needed, but a hard rule applies: NO overnight camping within a quarter mile of Cutthroat Lake. Camp outside that radius and you are legal with no paperwork.
bivy.capacity: Limited and regulated — the usable ground is set back from the water, so realistically a handful of small parties

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground
bivy.notes: The closest developed campground to the Cutthroat Creek trailhead, a short drive east on SR 20 along Early Winters Creek. Because nothing here can be booked, arriving Friday evening in July or August is a gamble and the fallback is dispersed camping on a spur road. The season runs roughly May or June through September or October, entirely dependent on when the highway opens and when snow returns.
bivy.water: Potable water provided in season, shut off once the campground closes for the year.
bivy.permit: No reservations and no permit — first-come, first-served with a nightly fee. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to camp, only to park at the trailhead.

bivy.name: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby
bivy.notes: Klipchuck sits about a quarter mile off SR 20 in fir and pine down-valley toward Mazama, low enough to be warm and dry when the passes are still wet. Early Winters Campground is further east, smaller at around a dozen tent sites, split by the highway near the Methow River, and fills quickly. Both are a longer drive to the trailhead than Lone Fir, which is the tradeoff for a better chance of finding a site on a busy weekend.
bivy.water: Drinking water spigots in season; vault toilets. Water is turned off at the end of the season while the sites stay usable.
bivy.permit: First-come, first-served, nightly fee, no reservation and no permit required.
bivy.capacity: 46 sites, the largest campground on this stretch of highway

bivy.name: Honeymoon Meadows
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and the last big established site on the West Fork, roughly eight trail-miles past the ranger station. Dry ground at the far end of the meadows once the snow goes. Getting here involves at least one calf- to knee-deep ford of the West Fork depending on melt, so arrive with time to deal with a high river rather than in the dark.

bivy.name: Camp Siberia / Anderson Pass shelter area
bivy.notes: PLANNED alternative about 0.7 mile and 700 ft above Honeymoon Meadows, below Anderson Pass. Sheltered and in trees, which is its value in weather — but parties routinely walk past it without finding it under snow, so do not commit to it as your only plan on a late arrival. It is still below the pass, so it leaves the whole climbers' path and moraine for the next day.
bivy.water: creek nearby
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required year-round for all overnight stays

bivy.name: Tarn camp above Anderson Pass
bivy.notes: PLANNED high camp and the one worth reaching — open slopes above Anderson/Valkyrie Lake, roughly a mile past the pass up the climbers' path and moraine, and preferred by parties specifically to avoid sleeping in the forest at or below the pass. Budget 7-9 hours from the road closure to here. This is the last water on the route: the snow finger to Flypaper Pass and everything on the Eel above it has none, so fill here or plan to melt. Exposed to wind, with no built shelter.
bivy.water: the tarn when melted out; often still frozen in spring, so melt snow
